extracted.intended_audience: patent drafters, patent attorneys, and applicants involved in drafting, filing, and prosecuting patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on drafting, filing (national, EPO, PCT), and prosecuting patent applications, including fee/translation planning, responding to office actions, amendment constraints, and strategic client advice. Covers procedural steps, documentation requirements, and common examination issues across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government and professional fees during prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: There are specific government fees for special procedures during the prosecution of an application (e.g., accelerated examination upon payment of a fee; extension of a time limit under certain conditions including payment). Most jurisdictions assess an issue fee to bring a patent into force and most charge some sort of maintenance fee to keep a patent in force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional fees may be significant at substantive examination because the drafter reviews prior art cited by the examiner and amends claims to overcome objections. Filing, searching and examination fees should generally be paid at filing; missing fees may incur surcharges or notices to submit fees. Consider the number and type of claims and small-entity status which can reduce government fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs of foreign filings and translations
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing patent applications in multiple national and regional patent offices can create substantial cumulative government fees and professional service fees; translations of the local application into languages accepted by foreign offices may be required and can be very costly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If drafting counterpart applications in multiple countries without a common language, multiple professional translations will be needed. Example: validating a European patent in four countries (Spain, Italy, Austria, Portugal) may require translations into multiple languages and total lifetime costs can exceed EUR 200,000. Patent drafters should advise clients on limiting filings to business-critical countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPO filing, designation, validation and translation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: EPO applications must use specific forms, pay fees, and submit various documents and translations (if necessary). Applications must indicate the Contracting States in which protection is sought; a single designation fee is charged regardless of number of states designated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After grant, the applicant must validate the European patent in each Contracting State chosen, typically involving payment of validation fees and required translations within time limits. Publication triggers the time limit for filing oppositions. Since April 2009 a single designation fee incentivizes designating all states to allow later country decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of PCT to postpone national-phase costs and gain time
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing under the PCT can be a good option from a costs perspective because the PCT allows postponement of the major costs associated with prosecution in foreign countries and grants at least 30 months (often more) from the initial filing to begin national prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PCT applications can be filed in any language accepted by the receiving office, but translations may be necessary if the language is not one of the PCT publication languages. The PCT effectively gains 18 months compared with Paris Convention 12-month priority window and postpones translation/validation/national fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advising clients strategically on international filing scope and fee reduction instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent drafters should provide sound advice about the costs of patent protection worldwide and offer ideas on how the client might limit costs by filing only in countries where protection is business-critical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advise clients about international instruments that reduce translation costs (e.g., London Agreement). Discuss strategic choices about which countries to pursue protection in and when to enter national phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. nonprovisional and provisional application content requirements (USPTO)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States, a nonprovisional patent application must include claims, an abstract, a description, an oath or declaration and, in most cases, drawings. A provisional application need not include claims and is primarily used to establish a priority date. Applications must be in English or accompanied by an English translation and a statement that the translation is accurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File a utility patent application transmittal form to identify the contents; use a fee transmittal to calculate fees and payment method. Small entity assertions halve certain government fees. An application data sheet should contain bibliographic data. Oath/declaration must be in a language the inventor understands; translations and accuracy statements required if not in English.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmittal and fee forms and small-entity/fee-payment practice (USPTO)
rubrics_metrics.description: A utility patent application transmittal form should be filed with every patent application to inform the USPTO what papers are being filed. A fee transmittal form may be used to calculate prescribed filing fees and indicate the method of payment. The amount payable depends on number/type of claims and small-entity status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing, searching and examination fees should be paid at filing; if not, applicant will be notified and asked to submit fees within a given period and surcharges may apply for late payment. Be mindful of whether mailing date or office action date determines time limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT international phase structure and core documents
rubrics_metrics.description: The PCT procedure consists of an international phase (including filing, international search and report, publication, optional supplementary search, optional international preliminary examination) and a later national phase. An international application must contain a request, a description, one or more claims, drawings where necessary, and an abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request form is available in all PCT publication languages and ePCT is available for online filing. The ISR and a preliminary nonbinding written opinion are issued by the ISA; if not withdrawn within 18 months the application and ISR are published.

rubrics_metrics.name: International search report (ISR) and written opinion as decision tools
rubrics_metrics.description: The international search is carried out by an ISA and results in an ISR — a list of published documents that might affect patentability — plus a preliminary and nonbinding written opinion on whether the invention appears to meet patentability criteria in light of the ISR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may withdraw, amend claims, or request further examination based on ISR/written opinion. The ISR/written opinion provide high-quality insight into likely patentability and help inform national-phase decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional supplementary international search (SIS) and international preliminary examination (IPEA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may request a supplementary international search (SIS) focusing on art in particular languages or jurisdictions (request within 22 months of priority). Applicants may also request an international preliminary examination to obtain another opinion on patentability as amended; this produces an international preliminary examination report (IPER).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SIS reduces likelihood of later-discovered relevant prior art in national phase. An IPER/IPRP Chapter I can strengthen the basis for proceeding in national/regional offices and allow further amendments during the international phase.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT fee categories and fee reductions
rubrics_metrics.description: During the PCT international phase applicants potentially pay (i) a transmittal fee to the receiving office, (ii) a search fee to the ISA, and (iii) an international filing fee to WIPO. Additional fees apply for optional SIS or international preliminary examination. National-phase fees are another set and are often the most expensive part of prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PCT reductions: 90% reduction on certain fees for natural persons from certain countries and for nationals/residents of least-developed countries; some ISAs reduce search fees for nationals/residents of certain countries. Many offices grant exemptions/reductions in national phase to natural persons, universities, not-for-profits, SMEs. Electronic filing often yields fee reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may file a PCT application and receiving-office rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Any national or resident of one of the PCT Contracting States may file. Where multiple applicants exist, at least one must be a national or resident of a Contracting State. An international application may be filed with the national patent office or with WIPO; often the national office acts as the receiving office. Nationals of regional patent organizations may file with the regional office where permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National security provisions may oblige filing a national patent application or requesting authorization before filing abroad. Ensure at least one acceptable language to ISA and PCT publication languages or provide translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages of filing under the PCT
rubrics_metrics.description: Main advantage is additional time to decide whether to prosecute in other countries (typically at least 30 months from initial filing), postponing costs of internationalizing a patent application and providing useful information (ISR and ISA written opinion) on likely patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PCT allows applicants to improve applications in international phase (correct formal defects, amend claims, file amendments during international preliminary examination), request bibliographic data changes, and benefits from safeguard measures protecting against losing rights due to procedural mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent prosecution as advocacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond preparing and filing a high-quality application, a patent drafter must skillfully and articulately advocate the patentability of the client’s invention before the examining office during substantive examination and in responses to office actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an examiner issues a negative office action, the drafter must prepare a respectful response explaining differences between invention and cited prior art and demonstrate patentability. Notify the client immediately and explain findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office actions represent the government’s official position
rubrics_metrics.description: An office action (official action/examination report) may address virtually any aspect of the application (title, abstract length, etc.), with most important parts touching on patentability of pending claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond promptly; failure to respond can impair rights. Understand the examiner’s cited prior art and the basis for enablement, novelty and inventive-step objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of examination rejections and appropriate rebuttals
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may issue enablement rejections (description insufficient), anticipation (prior art reads on claim), or obviousness (combination of prior art plus motivation to combine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebut by showing where description discloses subject matter, argue that alleged missing matter was known in prior art, argue examiner misunderstood prior art or the invention, argue lack of motivation to combine references, or amend claims to avoid cited art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be proactive in rebuttal and adducing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent drafter must not be passive; if the examiner misunderstood the invention or misjudged patentability, the drafter should counsel the client on rebuttal options including drawing examiner’s attention to additional information and documentation as evidence that claims should be allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience will teach when to concede and when to fight for better protection. Be mindful of foreign associates' work and when they may be following administrative efficiency suggestions rather than strict requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accelerated examination options including Patent Prosecution Highway (PPH)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent drafters may ask for accelerated examination if the patent office offers such services. The PPH program functions as an accelerated examination scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use accelerated options to obtain official actions earlier where strategic. Be aware of fees and criteria for accelerated programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to fully answer all examiner comments in responses
rubrics_metrics.description: A response must fully answer (respond to) all of the examiner’s comments set out in the office action. Failure to respond in full will likely render the response nonresponsive and lead to rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File complete responses; most offices impose time limits for filing responses (some without fee and extended periods with fee). Understand country-specific time periods and whether time runs from mailing date or office action date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limits and extensions for responding to office actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Most patent offices impose time limits to respond to office actions; some allow an initial period without fee and additional months with payment of extension fees. In some countries extensions are limited to certain circumstances; missing a deadline can lead to deemed withdrawal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the variety of time periods across offices; in the US typical office-action response is three months without fee plus three months with extension (total six). Confirm whether response period runs from mailing date or office action date in each jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client involvement and strategic choices when amending claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Drafter should explain draft response options to the client; amendments narrowing claims might overcome prior art but may render protection less useful because competitors can design around narrower claims. The client often best knows which additional claim element meets business needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give client opportunity to make choices regarding amendments; consider business objectives when narrowing or changing claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle prohibiting addition of new matter in amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal rule in most jurisdictions: no new matter (new subject matter) beyond that originally disclosed as of the filing date may be added to claims, description or drawings (except to remedy obvious mistakes such as typographic errors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule balances inventor/applicant interests and third-party predictability. Draft a complete disclosure prior to filing; if broad claims are not supported by original disclosure, later addition of new embodiments to justify breadth is not permitted. See Module VI for more on amending claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale for restricting amendments (policy justification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Restriction exists to prevent applicants from obtaining exclusive rights on subject matter not disclosed as of the filing date and to preserve the first-to-file principle and legal certainty for third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlimited post-filing amendments would allow effectively later inventions to be patented. This protects public notice and reliance on original disclosure timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining original disclosure and permissible post-filing changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners generally raise no objection to amendments that introduce further information regarding prior art, straightforwardly clarify obscure expressions, or resolve inconsistencies. However, most jurisdictions prohibit introduction of new matter into the description, drawings or claims after filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When amending, ensure added content is directly and unambiguously derivable from the application as filed. Clarifications and correcting inconsistencies are usually acceptable; substantive new embodiments or features not present in the original filing are not.
